subject: unordered categorical exogenous variables in observed variable models

messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: unordered categorical exogenous variables in observed variable models
parts:
So, I’ve seen questions about unordered categorical variables as exogenous variables in covariance-based model fits asked a few times on this list. There are two issues about their use:

1) They need to be converted into a set of binary 0/1 variables.

2) Even so, we have to drop one of the binary variables. Coefficients then need to be judged relative to the dropped variable - so-called Treatment contrasts, which we can see if we set meanstructure=TRUE.

I think I’ve come up to a hacky solution to both. #1 is easy and can be folded into a function. #2 is a bit of a pain, and I wonder if Yves might have a suggestion for making it easier or where it could be folded into the sem function.

Also note, this so far is for observed variable models only. Not sure how we would deal with this in a model with latent variables.

So, for #1, I’ve whipped up a function called makeBinaryTreatments.R which you can download at https://www.dropbox.com/s/nm773y2g13d7mn5/makeBinaryTreatments.R?dl=0

It will take a factor or character vector, and then turn it into a series of 0/1 numeric columns which you can cbind back to your original data set.

For #2, I realized that what you can do is give each coefficient a name, and also name the intercept coefficients. You can then calculate the net effect, instead of the relative effect, of each treatment as the sum of the intercept plus the estimated coefficient of the treatment using :=

Here’s an example for an experiment with three diet types (R, POLY, and MAPY) which influences the feeding rate and gonad development of sea urchins. For full context, see https://peerj.com/articles/719/

Data: https://www.dropbox.com/s/fy5big5sgbmb2tg/urchin_ex_sem.csv?dl=0
Code: https://www.dropbox.com/s/iojse6o7ybeuqxl/treatment_means.R?dl=0

#load libraries
library(lavaan)

#Make treatment into a series of binary variables
source("./makeBinaryTreatments.R")

#load data
urchinData<-read.csv("./urchin_ex_sem.csv")

#add binary treatment variables to data from a factor
binTrt<-makeBinaryTreatments(urchinData, "treatment")
urchinData<-cbind(urchinData, binTrt)

#The model - we have to drop one binary predictor
#so that the model can fit
urchinModel<-' 
Feeding.rate.dry ~ fm*MAPY + fr*R 
GONAD_INDEX ~ gm*MAPY + gr*R + Feeding.rate.dry 

Feeding.rate.dry ~ fi*1
GONAD_INDEX ~ gi*1


#derived variables show individual 
#treatment means
mapy_feeding := fm+fi
r_feeding := fr+fi
polt_feeding := fi

mapy_gonad := gm+gi
r_gonad := gi+gr
poly_gonad := gi

'

#Fit a model
urchinSEM<-sem(urchinModel, data=urchinData)

#unstandardized coefficients including mean effects
summary(urchinSEM)

#standardized coefficients
standardizedSolution(urchinSEM)

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: unordered categorical exogenous variables in observed variable models
parts:
Hi Jarrett,

Another approach to consider is to use what Green & Thompson (from the Handbook of SEM) call a Multiple Indicator Variable Approach. In this approach we fix the intercept to 0 and include all, k, binary predictors representing a categorical variable. This model is equivalent to a model with an intercept and k-1 binary predictors. The slopes for each of the binary indicators would be the group mean. In your example you could change the syntax to:

urchinModel<-' 
Feeding.rate.dry ~ MAPY + R + POLY 
GONAD_INDEX ~ MAPY + R + POLY+ Feeding.rate.dry 

Feeding.rate.dry ~ 0*1
GONAD_INDEX ~ 0*1
'

Alex

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: unordered categorical exogenous variables in observed variable models
parts: The slopes for each of the binary indicators would be the group mean.

Or the group intercept, if that variable has other predictors.  I agree with Alex that this is a great approach that makes parameters easier to interpret "as is" instead of relative to other values.  You can even incorporate interactions (product terms instead of a main effect) to define group-specific slopes, just like you would get in a multigroup model (except the single-group approach assumes homogeneous error variance).

Feeding.rate.dry ~ MAPY + R + POLY  # mean for each group
GONAD_INDEX ~ MAPY + R + POLY       # intercept for each group
## group-specific slopes
GONAD_INDEX ~ Feeding.rate.dry:MAPY + Feeding.rate.dry:R + Feeding.rate.dry:POLY
